topic: Lecture No. 1: Forensic Thanatology (4th-year General Medicine)

slides.title: Forensic Thanatology: Aims and Scope

bullets.text: Thanatology is the doctrine of death (Greek thanatos = death, logos = teaching). The term was introduced into medicine by I.I. Mechnikov.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: It studies the dying process, the clinical, morphological and biochemical changes in it, the fact of death, causes of death and post-mortem changes. It also covers the effect of external and internal factors and burial or preservation.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: General thanatology deals with the general features of these questions. Special thanatology looks at them for particular kinds of death.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Forensic thanatology is the part of the field that serves inquiry, investigation and court. Any doctor who may be called to act as an expert needs to know it.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 5 min. Discussion: Why does a clinician, not only a forensic expert, need thanatology? How does the 'special' branch differ from the 'general' one? Whiteboard task: write the Greek roots of 'thanatology' and list five topics it studies. Typical mistake: students think thanatology is only about the autopsy; it also covers dying, signs of death and cadaveric changes.

slides.title: Lecture Outline and Learning Outcomes

bullets.text: All doctors meet death and the dying, so they must know its medical and legal aspects.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Outcome: describe the stages of dying, the signs of death and the early and late cadaveric changes.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Outcome: estimate the post-mortem interval (PMI) with caution, since no single change gives a precise marker.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

diagram.caption: Lecture sequence

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 5 min. Discussion: Which step of the chain would a general practitioner meet first? Why is PMI estimation placed after cadaveric changes? Whiteboard task: draw the five-step chain and add one key term to each step. Typical mistake: students treat the sections as unrelated topics, although each step builds on the previous one.

slides.title: Death as a Process: Cellular and Somatic Death

bullets.text: Medically, death is a process, not a single event. Metabolism in different tissues and organs stops at different rates, which fuels ethical and moral debate about when death occurs.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Cellular death is the end of respiration and normal metabolism in cells, soon followed by autolysis and decay. Somatic death is the loss of integrated functioning of the whole person.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Cortical neurons die after only 3–7 minutes of complete oxygen deprivation. Skin and bone stay metabolically active for many hours, and their cells can be cultured days after somatic death.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: White blood cells can still move up to 12 hours after cardiac arrest. Microscopic identification of a 'vital reaction' to injury is therefore of doubtful reliability.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 7 min. Discussion: Why is it practical to separate cellular death from somatic death? How does the 12-hour survival of leukocytes affect the interpretation of a 'vital reaction'? Whiteboard task: make a two-column list of tissues that die early and those that survive long. Typical mistake: caution - cellular death is not the same as somatic death; the body dies cell by cell and the whole process may take many hours.

slides.title: Defining Death: Irreversibility and Brain Death

bullets.text: Death is a process, not a single event: cells and organs stop at different rates. So cellular death and somatic death (loss of integrated function of the person) are considered separately.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Somatic death means irreversible unconsciousness with no further interaction with the environment. Deep sleep, anaesthesia, drugs or temporary coma look similar but are reversible.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Ventilation breaks the old chain 'brain-stem death, apnoea, myocardial hypoxia, cardiac arrest'. A ventilated patient can keep a beating heart after brain-stem function has irreversibly stopped.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: In the local textbook, death of the cerebral cortex marks the start of biological ('brain') death. Other organs may still work, which makes organ retrieval for transplantation possible.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 8 min. Discussion: Why is the word 'irreversible' the key to the definition of death? Why can a person on a ventilator still have a heartbeat after brain death? Whiteboard task: draw the old chain of events and mark where artificial ventilation interrupts it. Typical mistake: students equate the end of the heartbeat with death of all cells; cells die one by one over hours.

slides.title: Terminal States: Stages of Dying

bullets.text: Preagony: depressed CNS, falling blood pressure, acidosis and hypoxia; pulse is felt only in large arteries.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Terminal pause: breathing stops suddenly and pupils dilate and fixate. Agony: lower brain centres briefly restore breathing and pulse.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Caution: the first four states can be reversible; biological death, with irreversible brain changes, is not.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

diagram.caption: Sequence of terminal states with typical duration

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 8 min. Discussion: Which stage is the last chance for resuscitation? Why is agony called a last attempt of the body to survive? Whiteboard task: reproduce the five-step chain and write one key sign for each step. Typical mistake: confusing the terminal pause (seconds to minutes, no breathing) with agony (breathing returns).

slides.title: Clinical Death and Resuscitation

bullets.text: Clinical death starts when the heart stops. Brain and brain stem are deeply impaired, but their function can still be restored, while individual organs keep working.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: In usual conditions it lasts up to 5-6 minutes, then irreversible cortical changes develop. In cold it may extend to 30 minutes; cause, age and health also matter.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Cortical neurons die after only 3-7 minutes of complete oxygen deprivation. Modern ventilation and support save patients who would once have died from brain injury or hypoxia.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: The possibility of revival founded resuscitation science. At the end of agony the dying face shows facies hippocratica: pale, earthy, sunken eyes, drooping jaw, open mouth.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: Why does cold prolong the reversible period? How does the 5-6 min limit relate to cortical neuron death? Whiteboard task: list factors that shorten or lengthen clinical death. Typical mistake: treating the 5-6 minute figure as an exact limit; it is an average that depends on conditions.

slides.title: Types of Agony and Rate of Dying

bullets.text: Rapid death: the agonal period is absent or very short. Slow death: agony may last days to weeks, so it is also called agonal death.

source.author: Ромодановский П.О., Баринов Е.Х.
source.title: Судебная медицина в схемах и рисунках: учебное пособие, М.: Проспект (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

bullets.text: Agony is a last struggle: lower brain centres take over, and breathing and pulse briefly return.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Rapid death is typical of electrical injury, mechanical asphyxia and anaphylactic shock.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

diagram.caption: Four types of agony (Lawes and Berg, 1965)
rows: Body disruption, injuries incompatible with life

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: Why does the tempo of dying matter to a forensic expert? How does artificial prolongation of agony change the interpretation of findings at autopsy? Whiteboard task: draw a timeline from pre-agony to biological death and mark where agony falls. Typical mistake: treating agony as a sign of recovery; it is the last attempt at survival and usually ends in death.

slides.title: Morphological Signs of Rapid vs Slow Dying

bullets.text: Blood stays liquid in rapid death because of fibrinolysis; with a long agony, clots may form after about 2 hours.

source.author: Пиголкин Ю.И., Баринов Е.Х., Богомолов Д.В., Богомолова И.Н.
source.title: Судебная медицина: учебник для вузов, М.: ГЭОТАР-МЕД (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

bullets.text: The longer the agony, the more fibrin-rich clots and the stronger the dystrophic changes in internal organs.

source.author: Пиголкин Ю.И., Баринов Е.Х., Богомолов Д.В., Богомолова И.Н.
source.title: Судебная медицина: учебник для вузов, М.: ГЭОТАР-МЕД (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

bullets.text: Caution: these findings indicate the tempo of dying, not the cause of death.

source.author: Ромодановский П.О., Баринов Е.Х.
source.title: Судебная медицина в схемах и рисунках: учебное пособие, М.: Проспект (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

diagram.caption: Findings by tempo of dying
rows: Red and yellow clots in heart and vessels
Petechiae in eyes, mucosae, pleura, epicardium
Not typical; oedema of lungs and brain

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 7 min. Discussion: Which finding is the most reliable sign of a short agonal period? Why can sudden death leave involuntary urination, defecation or emission of semen? Whiteboard task: reproduce the comparison table from memory. Typical mistake: using petechiae alone to diagnose asphyxia; they only suggest rapid dying.

slides.title: Case Analysis: Rate of Dying

bullets.text: Scenario: a man collapses at work and dies within minutes. No illness is documented, and no clear injury is visible.

source.author: Харин Г.М. (Kharin G.M.)
source.title: Краткий курс судебной медицины: учебное пособие, М.: ГЭОТАР-Медиа (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

bullets.text: At autopsy: liquid blood in the heart and large vessels, petechiae in the conjunctivae and serous membranes, abundant dark violet lividity.

source.author: Харин Г.М. (Kharin G.M.)
source.title: Краткий курс судебной медицины: учебное пособие, М.: ГЭОТАР-Медиа (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

bullets.text: Also found: marked venous congestion of internal organs and little dystrophy. Question: what tempo of dying do these findings suggest?

source.author: Ромодановский П.О., Баринов Е.Х.
source.title: Судебная медицина в схемах и рисунках: учебное пособие, М.: Проспект (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

bullets.text: Answer: rapid death with a very short or absent agony. The cause must still be established by full examination.

source.author: Пиголкин Ю.И., Баринов Е.Х., Богомолов Д.В., Богомолова И.Н.
source.title: Судебная медицина: учебник для вузов, М.: ГЭОТАР-МЕД (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: Which findings would make you doubt rapid death (for example, firm clots or marked oedema)? What further examinations are needed to name the cause? Whiteboard task: list findings for and against a short agonal period. Typical mistake: concluding the cause of death (for example asphyxia) from tempo findings alone.

slides.title: Vegetative State and Permanent Vegetative State

bullets.text: In the vegetative state (VS), resuscitation keeps brain-stem function but cortical function is lost: wakefulness without awareness. The patient may recover or move into a minimally conscious state (MCS).

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Under Royal College of Physicians guidelines (2003), VS is judged permanent after 12 months if caused by traumatic brain injury, or after 6 months if the cause was non-traumatic.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: In permanent VS, withdrawal of hydration and assisted nutrition can be considered in the patient's 'best interests'. The leading case is Airedale NHS Trust v Bland (Tony Bland), where withdrawal of feeding was permitted.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Caution: common error – VS is not brain-stem death. In VS the brain-stem still works; in brain-stem death its function is irreversibly lost.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 4 min. Discussion: (1) Why do the time limits differ for traumatic and non-traumatic causes? (2) What ethical issues arise when feeding is withdrawn? Whiteboard task: draw a spectrum from full recovery to MCS, VS and brain-stem death. Typical mistake: students equate VS with brain death. Optional point: functional MRI has shown that some patients labelled VS have brain activity closer to MCS; none has recovered beyond that state, so law and practice may change (Simpson's, p. 26).

slides.title: Euthanasia: Types and Terminology

bullets.text: The term was introduced by the English philosopher Francis Bacon in the 16th century (Greek eu = good, thanatos = death).

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: The original meaning is to ease the suffering of patients who are doomed to die.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Many authors use a narrow meaning: only active and passive euthanasia, i.e. hastening death by action or by omission.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

diagram.caption: Four types of euthanasia (after the local textbook)
rows: Act that hastens death (with or without intent)
Limiting or stopping care for the dying
Failure of duty or endangering life
Drugs ease suffering, improve life quality

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 5 min. Discussion: (1) Why is a large analgesic dose given to relieve pain classed as indirect active euthanasia and not as murder? (2) How does dysthanasia differ from medicotanasia? Whiteboard task: place each example on a line from 'hastening death' to 'prolonging life'. Typical mistake: mixing up direct and indirect active euthanasia – the difference is the intent to hasten death. Note: this classification comes from the local textbook (G‘iyosov); it is not in Simpson's.

slides.title: Brain-Stem Death Criteria and Prerequisites

bullets.text: Absent: pupil, corneal, oculovestibular, cough and gag reflexes; no cranial-nerve motor response.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Apnoea test: no breathing after ventilator disconnection, with PaCO2 rising by over 0.5 kPa.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Prerequisites: known irreversible brain damage; drugs, hypothermia, metabolic and endocrine causes excluded.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

diagram.caption: Sequence of brain-stem death diagnosis

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: (1) Why must depressant drugs and hypothermia be excluded before testing? (2) Why can brain-stem tests be impossible in extensive maxillofacial injury? Whiteboard task: list the reflexes tested and the nerve or pathway each one involves. Typical mistake: forgetting that neuromuscular blocking agents are a reversible cause of apnoea that must be excluded. Source detail (Simpson's, pp. 25-26): the doctors must be registered for more than 5 years and competent in these tests; ancillary investigations are cerebral angiography, perfusion and neurophysiological tests.

slides.title: Confirming Death after Cardiorespiratory Arrest

bullets.text: Death is confirmed when apnoea and unconsciousness begin together and irreversibly, with no circulation, after full attempts to reverse any contributing cause.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: One of three conditions must apply: CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) is not indicated, CPR has failed, or life-sustaining treatment was withdrawn as not in the patient's best interest or by advance decision.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: The certifying person observes for at least 5 minutes, finding no central pulse on palpation and no heart sounds on auscultation. Pupils must not react to light, with no corneal reflex or motor response to supra-orbital pressure.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: In hospital, supporting evidence may be asystole on a continuous ECG (electrocardiogram), no contractile activity on echocardiography, or no pulsatile flow on intra-arterial monitoring. The time of death is recorded once criteria are met.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: Why must the loss of function be irreversible, not just present? Why is 5 minutes of observation required? Whiteboard task: list the bedside checks in the order you would perform them. Typical mistake: students treat ECG asystole as mandatory, but in the source it is only supplementary evidence in hospital.

slides.title: Organ and Tissue Transplantation

bullets.text: Sources of grafts: homologous (same body, e.g. skin or bone chips), live donation (blood, marrow, kidney, part of liver), cadaveric donation, xenografts (animal tissue) and, in theory, cloning.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Cadaveric organs work best when taken during circulation or right after it stops, to keep 'warm ischaemic time' short. Kidneys tolerate anoxia better and can survive up to 30 minutes after cardiac activity ceases.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Systems differ: some countries allow removal regardless of relatives, others use 'opting out' (removal unless relatives object). The UK uses 'opting in': prior permission or no objection, and no close relative objecting.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: If an autopsy is required by law, the coroner or other legal officer must permit harvesting first. Xenografts raise viral-transmission risk, and selling kidneys is illegal in many countries and unethical.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 7 min. Discussion: Which consent system (opting in or opting out) better serves patients, and why? Why do legal officers rarely object to donation? Whiteboard task: draw a table of the five graft sources with one example each. Typical mistake: confusing homologous (same body) with allograft from another person, or confusing opting in with opting out.

slides.title: Case Analysis: Declaring Death and Donation

bullets.text: Scenario: a man with severe head trauma is on a ventilator. Before brain-stem testing, doctors must exclude depressant drugs, hypothermia, metabolic or endocrine disturbance and neuromuscular blockers as causes of coma.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Two doctors registered for over 5 years, one a consultant, test the reflexes. Pupils, corneal, oculovestibular, cough and gag reflexes are absent, and the apnoea test shows PaCO2 rising more than 0.5 kPa.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: The family agrees to donation, but the death is a suspected assault requiring autopsy. The coroner's permission is needed before organs are harvested, and the pathologist may attend retrieval.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Question: why does artificial ventilation make the old 'respiratory arrest then cardiac arrest' chain unreliable, and which test shows brain-stem death despite a beating heart?

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 8 min. Discussion: What could go wrong if hypothermia or sedatives were not excluded? Who should give permission for donation here? Whiteboard task: write the sequence from exclusion of reversible causes to recording the time of death. Typical mistake: starting reflex testing before excluding drugs and metabolic causes.

slides.title: Quick Question: Death and Dying

bullets.text: Q1: Name the terminal states in order. A: pre-agony, terminal pause, agony, clinical death, then biological death.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Q2: How long does clinical death normally last? A: about 5-6 minutes, after which irreversible cortical changes develop. Cold can extend this period to up to 30 minutes.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Q3: How quickly do cortical neurons die without oxygen? A: after only 3-7 minutes of complete oxygen deprivation, while skin and bone cells stay metabolically active for hours.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Q4: Why is 'irreversible' the key word in somatic death? A: deep sleep, anaesthesia, drugs or temporary coma also stop communication with the environment, but they are reversible.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 5 min. Discuss: (1) Why is death a process rather than a single event? (2) Why does the resuscitation concept depend on clinical death? Whiteboard task: draw the five terminal stages in a row and mark which are potentially reversible. Typical mistake: students confuse clinical death with biological death, or treat the cessation of the heartbeat as final.

slides.title: Presumptive and Reliable Signs of Death

bullets.text: Presumptive signs (immobility, pallor, no breathing or pulse) appear at once but are not conclusive.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Beloglazov's sign ('cat's eye'): the pupil turns oval when the eyeball is squeezed. It is the earliest reliable sign, at about 15-20 minutes.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Caution: pseudodeath (electric shock, sleeping-pill poisoning, heatstroke) can mimic death, so do not rely on pulse and breathing alone.

source.author: Харин Г.М. (Kharin G.M.)
source.title: Краткий курс судебной медицины: учебное пособие, М.: ГЭОТАР-Медиа (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

diagram.caption: Reliable signs and approximate timing

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 8 min. Discuss: (1) Why are presumptive signs not enough to certify death? (2) In which situations might a doctor wrongly declare death? Whiteboard task: list presumptive signs on the left and reliable signs on the right, with times. Typical mistake: treating the timings as exact; they are only approximate guidelines and vary with temperature and other conditions.

slides.title: Forensic Classification of Death

bullets.text: Category: violent death results from external factors; non-violent death results from disease.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Kind (homicide, suicide, accident) is decided by investigators, because it rests on proving intent.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Caution: 'kind' is not 'type'. Type names the causative factor, e.g. mechanical injury, asphyxia, poisoning, temperature or electricity.

source.author: Харин Г.М. (Kharin G.M.)
source.title: Краткий курс судебной медицины: учебное пособие, М.: ГЭОТАР-Медиа (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

diagram.caption: Levels of forensic classification of death
rows: By disease: heart, lung, digestive, etc.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 7 min. Discuss: (1) Why does the expert not decide whether a death is homicide or suicide? (2) Give an example of a violent death whose type is asphyxia. Whiteboard task: classify three short scenarios by category, kind and type. Typical mistake: mixing up 'kind' and 'type', since both terms are used loosely in everyday speech.

slides.title: Cause of Death, Mechanism and Thanatogenesis

bullets.text: Thanatogenesis: a causal chain; the first link is the initial cause, the last link the immediate cause.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Stab wound of the right atrium: chest wound, then haemopericardium, then cardiac compression.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Competing causes: two independently lethal conditions, e.g. head injury plus drowning.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

diagram.caption: Chain of death: peptic ulcer example

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 8 min. Discussion: (1) Why must the expert name the initial cause first in the forensic diagnosis? (2) How can the same disease lead to different immediate causes, e.g. a bleeding ulcer causing post-haemorrhagic shock? Whiteboard task: students draw the chain for the stab wound of the right atrium and label initial, intermediate and immediate causes. Typical mistake: treating the immediate cause (e.g. sepsis) as the initial cause.

slides.title: Death Certification and Medico-legal Investigation

bullets.text: The WHO certificate has two parts. Part I lists the causally linked conditions leading directly to death, lines (a), (b), (c). Part II lists other contributing conditions. The lowest Part I disease is the primary cause.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Each condition has a four-digit ICD code, which makes data comparable between countries. In many Western systems a legal officer, not the doctor, decides the manner of death.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: In England and Wales, deaths that are violent, unnatural, sudden of unknown cause or in custody go to the Coroner. A death must also be referred if the doctor did not see the patient within 14 days before death.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: An inquest asks who died, and when, where and how. Verdicts include unlawful killing, accident, suicide, natural causes and open verdict. They must not imply blame.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 8 min. Discussion: (1) Why is the lowest line of Part I the most important for statistics? (2) Why does the Coroner's court avoid expressing criminal or civil blame? Whiteboard task: draw an empty two-part certificate and fill lines Ia-Ic with an example of your own. Typical mistake: using Part II as a list of every disease the patient had, regardless of its role in the death.

slides.title: Case Analysis: Certifying the Cause of Death

bullets.text: Scenario: a patient dies in coma after a subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured congenital aneurysm. How should Part I of the certificate be written?

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Answer: Ia Coma; Ib Subarachnoid haemorrhage; Ic Ruptured congenital aneurysm. Line (c), the lowest, is the primary condition used for mortality statistics.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Caution: common error. Writing only a mode of death, such as 'coma' or 'heart failure', is wrong. A mode must be tied to the underlying pathological abnormality.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Question for students: if only 'Ia Cardiac failure' were written, what information would be lost for statistics and for the Coroner?

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 7 min. Discussion: (1) Why does a mode alone fail to identify the primary disease? (2) How does this certification logic relate to the thanatogenesis chain in Russian-language and local textbooks? Whiteboard task: students write the chain for a death from cardiac failure due to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Typical mistake: placing the mode of death on the lowest line instead of the underlying disease.

slides.title: Early Post-mortem Changes: Overview

bullets.text: Eyes: corneal and pupillary reflexes vanish; retinal blood columns fragment ('trucking'); tension falls.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Muscles go flaccid but may twitch or react to taps for some hours; skin and mucosae turn pale.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Urine voiding, semen emission and gastric regurgitation are common and prove nothing about the cause.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

diagram.caption: Main early changes (first day) and their limits
rows: Onset time too variable for PMI
Most useful PMI marker, still approximate

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: Why is a doctor expected to know the normal early changes? Which findings could be mistaken for injury or asphyxia? Whiteboard task: draw the chain from cardiac arrest to rigor, livor and cooling. Typical mistake: treating vomit in the airway or semen as proof of cause of death or recent sexual activity.

slides.title: Supravital Reactions

bullets.text: Some tissues still react to stimuli for hours after death; the reaction fades with time and helps date death.

source.author: Ромодановский П.О., Баринов Е.Х.
source.title: Судебная медицина в схемах и рисунках: учебное пособие, М.: Проспект (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

bullets.text: A tap on the biceps raises an idiomuscular ridge that shrinks, then becomes a dent by about 10-11 hours.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Caution: white cells can move up to 12 h after arrest, so microscopic 'vital reactions' are doubtful.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

diagram.caption: Supravital tests (approximate windows from local textbooks)
rows: Ridge to ~9 h; dent to ~11 h
Face 2-3 h; eye muscles to 11-12 h
Slower with time; up to ~24 h

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 7 min. Discussion: Why do supravital reactions fade in a fixed order? Why can they give only a rough PMI? Whiteboard task: draw a time axis 0-12 h and mark when each reaction ends. Typical mistake: using one textbook's figures as exact; ranges differ between sources and depend on temperature.

slides.title: Post-mortem Cooling (Algor Mortis)

bullets.text: By Newton's law heat passes from the warm body to cooler surroundings. A body cools unevenly and each body lies in its own environment, so rates differ.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Textbooks quote about 1 degree C per hour at room temperature, but Simpson's calls such rules of thumb too unreliable to use.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Three assumptions: body temperature was 37 C at death; a few readings can be extrapolated by formula; the environment stayed thermally constant.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Rate depends on mass, clothing, fat, posture and air movement. Rectal probing may spoil forensic samples; nose or ear readings differ from deep rectal or liver values.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 7 min. Discussion: Which of the three assumptions is most often violated at a scene? Why should the first police officers record the ambient temperature and time? Whiteboard task: list factors that slow cooling and factors that speed it. Typical mistake: assuming a body is at 37 C at death or using 'warm to touch' as evidence of time of death.

slides.title: Post-mortem Drying

bullets.text: After death the glands stop secreting and moisture evaporates. Drying first appears on naturally moist surfaces: the red lip margin, mucosae, cornea, conjunctiva and scrotal skin.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Areas with damaged epidermis also dry early: abrasions, wound edges and ligature furrows. With the eyes open, the cornea clouds in 1-3 h and Larche spots appear at the sides by 4-5 h.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Dried injured skin becomes firm and yellow-brown (parchment patch). Test: put gauze soaked in warm saline on it for 5-10 min. A parchment patch softens and pales; a vital abrasion does not change.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Caution: hair does not grow after death. Dry, retracted skin only makes the beard look more prominent, especially against pale skin.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 5 min. Discussion: Why do the lip margin and scrotum dry first? How would you distinguish a post-mortem abrasion from a vital one at the scene? Whiteboard task: list the body sites that dry first and the time of Larche spots. Typical mistake: believing that hair and nails keep growing after death.

slides.title: Rigor Mortis: Mechanism and Course

bullets.text: Guide times in temperate conditions: face 1-4 h, limbs 3-6 h, maximum about 18 h, gone after about 50 h.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Faster with exercise, low glycogen, electrocution or heat; slower but longer in the cold.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Test across a joint with gentle pressure only. If rigor is broken by force, that muscle group cannot be reliably tested again.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

diagram.caption: Chain of events in rigor mortis

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: Why does rigor appear first in small muscles? Why does a hot environment shorten its duration? Whiteboard task: draw the chain from lack of oxygen to stiffness and mark the timeline 1-4 h, 3-6 h, 18 h, 50 h. Typical mistake: treating the times as exact limits or saying that muscles shorten without tension.

slides.title: Cadaveric Rigidity and Caution on Rigor

bullets.text: Cadaveric rigidity is stiffness said to begin at the moment of death. It is shown by objects gripped in the hand, such as weeds in a drowned person or a trigger in a suicidal shooting.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Its mechanism is unexplained, possibly neurogenic, so 'instantaneous rigor' is a poor term. Local sources link a cataleptic form to medulla, cervical cord or solar plexus injury and convulsant poisoning.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Caution: stiffness from severe cold or freezing is not rigor. It disappears when the body warms in the mortuary, and true rigor may develop afterwards.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Rigor is very variable and gives only a rough estimate of the post-mortem interval (PMI). Charts that assign times to the degree of rigor should be viewed with scepticism.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 5 min. Discussion: How would you tell cold stiffening from true rigor at a winter scene? Why is cadaveric rigidity not the same process as rigor? Whiteboard task: two columns comparing rigor mortis and cadaveric rigidity. Typical mistake: using the degree of rigor alone to give an exact time of death.

slides.title: Post-mortem Lividity (Hypostasis)

bullets.text: Gravity settles red cells in the lowest vessels; the colour shows through the skin as lividity.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Pressed or clothed areas stay pale; the site follows body position (hanging: legs and arms).

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: CO: cherry-pink; cyanide: brick-red. Colour alone never proves the cause of death.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

diagram.caption: Three stages of lividity
rows: Disappears, returns quickly; moves if body turned
Only pales, recovers slowly; partial shift

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: (1) Why is lividity absent in severe blood loss or anaemia? (2) Why can lividity not date death precisely? Whiteboard: draw a supine body and shade the lividity and the pale pressure areas. Typical mistake: treating lividity colour as proof of cause of death. Note: Simpson's calls cyanide lividity brick-red, whereas G'iyosov's textbook calls it cherry-red; state that colour is only a clue.

slides.title: Lividity versus Bruises; Autolysis

bullets.text: Caution: lividity is not a bruise; make a cross-shaped incision in the doubtful area.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Autolysis begins in enzyme-rich tissues: stomach and gut mucosa, pancreas, adrenal medulla.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Autolysed gastric mucosa can be mistaken for corrosive poisoning; the pancreas may mimic necrosis.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

diagram.caption: Lividity compared with a bruise

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: (1) Why can lay people mistake lividity for bruising? (2) Which methods separate autolytic from vital changes? (Microscopy.) Whiteboard: list the four comparison features. Typical mistake: judging by colour alone without incision; also reading autolytic gastric changes as poisoning.

slides.title: Case Analysis: Lividity and Body Position

bullets.text: Scenario: an adult is found face down on a bed. The face is congested with petechiae; the skin around the nose and mouth is pale, with linear marks from blanket creases.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: The pallor comes from pressure against the bedding and the congestion from hypostasis in lax facial tissue. Neither proves suffocation; neck, nose and mouth must be dissected to exclude pressure.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Compare: a hanged body has lividity in the lower legs and arms but none on the torso; a body slipped head-first off a bed shows it on the head and upper chest.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Question: the body is turned onto its back during the first hours. Where will the lividity be, and how does the stage of lividity change your answer?

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 7 min. Answer: in hypostasis the lividity fades and reappears on the new dependent side; in stasis it shifts only partly, so two overlapping patterns are seen; in imbibition it stays where it is. Discussion: what findings would support or exclude smothering? Whiteboard: sketch the pattern for a hanged body and for a body face down. Typical mistake: calling facial petechiae and pallor around the nose proof of suffocation without dissection.

slides.title: Late Changes: Putrefaction

bullets.text: Greening starts in the right iliac fossa, where gut bacteria spread into the skin and break down haemoglobin.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Warmer temperature means earlier and faster putrefaction; no reliable timetable for decomposition exists.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Casper's ratio: decay in air : water : earth = 1 : 2 : 8 (twice slower in water, eight times slower in earth).

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

diagram.caption: Typical sequence of putrefaction (timings vary with conditions)

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: Why does greening begin in the right iliac fossa? Why can purge fluid be mistaken for injury? Whiteboard task: draw the body with the sequence greening, marbling, blisters, bloating, and add Casper's ratio 1:2:8. Typical mistake: treating the day numbers as exact; sources differ (G‘iyosov gives day 2 for greening, Simpson 3–4 days) because temperature and environment change the pace.

slides.title: Preservative Changes: Adipocere, Mummification, Peat Tanning

bullets.text: Adipocere (body fat hydrolysed to a soap-like wax) usually takes weeks to months; it is reported as early as 3 weeks.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Mummification is complete in adults in about 6–12 months and in young children in 4–6 months; in very favourable conditions, 2–3 months.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Artificial changes: embalming and freezing preserve the body; dismemberment, burning and dissolving destroy it.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

diagram.caption: Preservative changes compared
rows: Grey, waxy; complete in adult ~10–12 months
Dry, hard, brown; body weight falls
Dark brown hard skin; soft, cuttable bones
Body may keep its form for years

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: Why does adipocere need water but mummification needs dry air? Why are these called preservative rather than destructive changes? Whiteboard task: draw a wet-to-dry axis and place adipocere, peat tanning, mummification on it. Typical mistake: assuming the whole body is always uniformly affected; Simpson notes that adipocere, mummification and putrefaction can coexist in one body.

slides.title: Insects, Animals and Skeletalization

bullets.text: Flies lay eggs on moist sites (eyes, nose, mouth, wounds); larvae moult through instars, then pupate. The cycle takes about 21–24 days, depending on species and temperature.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: Under favourable conditions fly larvae can strip an adult's soft tissue in 4–6 weeks; beetle larvae follow (necrophagous 30–45 days, predatory 45–60 days).

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Caution: animal predation can mimic injury. Rat-bite margins show no bleeding or reddening, yet post-mortem wounds may bleed; doubtful bite marks need an odontologist.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: In a formally buried body soft tissue is usually gone by about 2 years; by about 5 years the bones are bare and disarticulated. Dating bones needs an anthropologist.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: Why do insects help to estimate the post-mortem interval (PMI) while damage by larger animals does not? How would you tell an animal bite from an injury inflicted in life? Whiteboard task: draw the fly cycle egg, larva (instars), pupa, adult with approximate timings. Typical mistake: saying that post-mortem injuries never bleed; they can, especially on the scalp and in bodies recovered from water.

slides.title: Estimating the Post-mortem Interval

bullets.text: Henssge's nomogram is the most useful method; its 95% accuracy is at best ±2.8 hours.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: A 5°C error in the ambient temperature shifts the likely time of death by at least 1 hour.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

bullets.text: No single method is reliable; combine methods. Precision falls from hours to days to years as time passes.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

diagram.caption: Henssge nomogram: worked example from the book

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 6 min. Discussion: (1) Why does the nomogram need body weight and ambient temperature? (2) Why is the spread of about 5.5 hours still useful to an investigator? Whiteboard task: draw the three inputs (rectal temperature, ambient temperature, body weight) and the output range. Typical mistake: quoting the single 'most likely' time without the 95% range. Also note that the nomogram assumes a naked body lying in still air and needs corrective factors for clothing or draughts. It should not be used where there is strong radiation, fever or hypothermia, or where cooling conditions changed.

slides.title: Quick Question and Case: PMI Calculation

bullets.text: Case: rectum 30°C at 10:00 and 28.2°C at 12:00, i.e. 1.8°C lost in 2 h (0.9°C per hour).

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Book's answer: death 7–7.5 h before 10:00; rules of thumb are unreliable, so cross-check.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

bullets.text: Quick question: why take two readings 1–1.5 h apart and record the air temperature?

source.author: Харин Г.М. (Kharin G.M.)
source.title: Краткий курс судебной медицины: учебное пособие, М.: ГЭОТАР-Медиа (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

diagram.caption: Lividity pressure test by stage (approximate)

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 8 min. Discussion: (1) Why does the rate of cooling change over time rather than staying at 0.9°C per hour? (2) What would you do if the two readings were taken with different thermometers or at different sites? Whiteboard task: students calculate the cooling rate from the two readings and compare it with the room-temperature rule of about 1°C per hour. The book's answer of 7–7.5 hours is not fully derivable from the printed text, so treat it as an illustration and check it with Henssge's nomogram. Typical errors: using one reading only; assuming 37°C at death without caution; ignoring the ambient temperature. Caution: lividity that does not blanch (imbibition) will not move when the body is turned, whereas early lividity shifts. Stage timings vary between textbooks, so use them as guidelines only.

slides.title: Scene Examination and Body at the Scene

bullets.text: Static stage: record the scene untouched; dynamic stage: objects and body are moved and studied.

source.author: Харин Г.М. (Kharin G.M.)
source.title: Краткий курс судебной медицины: учебное пособие, М.: ГЭОТАР-Медиа (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

bullets.text: Doctor's tasks: confirm death, record changes, help find and collect biological traces, advise investigator.

source.author: Харин Г.М. (Kharin G.M.)
source.title: Краткий курс судебной медицины: учебное пособие, М.: ГЭОТАР-Медиа (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

bullets.text: Evidence: clothing wrapped with traces inward and sealed; body wrapped to keep microparticles.

source.author: Ромодановский П.О., Баринов Е.Х.
source.title: Судебная медицина в схемах и рисунках: учебное пособие, М.: Проспект (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

bullets.text: Dying is a process: preagony, terminal pause, agony, clinical death (about 5-6 minutes in usual conditions), then biological death.

slides.teacher_notes: Time: 5 min. Discussion: (1) Which findings at a scene help most to estimate the post-mortem interval (PMI), and why is a single sign unreliable? (2) How do death certification and autopsy complement each other? Whiteboard task: students draw the chain from dying to late post-mortem changes with approximate times. Typical mistake: quoting a precise time of death from one finding such as rigor or body temperature alone.

mcq.question: A pathologist notes that white blood cells are still motile about 10 hours after cardiac arrest. What does this finding mean for the microscopic identification of a 'vital reaction' to injury?
options: It proves that the injury was inflicted after death
It makes the reliability of this concept doubtful
It confirms that the injury occurred just before death
It shows that cortical neurons are still alive
mcq.explanation: White blood cells can move for up to about 12 hours after cardiac arrest. A cellular response can therefore be seen after somatic death, so the microscopic 'vital reaction' is of doubtful reliability. Cortical neurons, by contrast, die after only 3-7 minutes without oxygen.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: A patient is deeply anaesthetised and does not communicate or react to the environment. Why is this patient NOT considered to be in somatic death?
options: Because the heart is still beating in this state
Because the pupils still react to light in this state
Because brain-stem reflexes are always present in this state
Because the loss of interaction with the environment is reversible
mcq.explanation: Somatic death means the person will never again communicate or interact with the environment. The key word is 'irreversible'. Deep sleep, anaesthesia, drug or alcohol effects and temporary coma also cause lack of interaction, but they are reversible.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: A dying patient has no consciousness, no reflexes, no pulse and no breathing, and the blood pressure is close to zero. The state lasts only seconds to 3-4 minutes. Which stage of dying is this?
options: Terminal pause
Preagonal state
Agony
Biological death
mcq.explanation: In the terminal pause, breathing stops suddenly, cardiac activity is severely disturbed, the pupils dilate and reflexes fade. It lasts from a few seconds to 3-4 minutes. The preagonal state still has a weak pulse in large arteries, and agony shows a temporary return of breathing and blood pressure.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

mcq.question: A young man collapses with cardiac arrest in a room at normal temperature. Within approximately what time do irreversible changes develop in the cerebral cortex, ending the period of clinical death?
options: About 1-2 minutes
About 15-20 minutes
About 5-6 minutes
About 30 minutes
mcq.explanation: Under ordinary conditions clinical death lasts up to 5-6 minutes, after which irreversible changes develop in the cortex. Only at low temperatures can it extend to about 30 minutes.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

mcq.question: At autopsy the blood in the heart is liquid, there are petechiae in the conjunctivae and under the pleura, and the livor mortis is confluent and dark violet. What rate of dying do these findings suggest?
options: Long agonal period with red and yellow blood clots
Rapid dying with a short or absent agonal period
Artificially prolonged agony lasting for weeks
Slow dying with severe dystrophic organ changes
mcq.explanation: Liquid blood, petechial haemorrhages, venous congestion and abundant dark-violet livor mortis are typical of rapid dying with a short agonal period. A long agonal period is marked by clots, moderate lividity and pronounced oedema or dystrophic changes.

source.author: Ромодановский П.О., Баринов Е.Х.
source.title: Судебная медицина в схемах и рисунках: учебное пособие, М.: Проспект (egasi taqdim etgan; yopiq foydalanish)

mcq.question: A comatose patient on a ventilator after a severe head injury is being assessed for brain-stem death. Which of the following must be excluded BEFORE the brain-stem tests are started?
options: Fixed pupils that do not react to light
Depressant drugs or hypothermia as the cause of coma
Absence of the corneal reflex on testing
Absence of a cough reflex on suction
mcq.explanation: Before brain-stem testing, potentially reversible causes of coma must be excluded. These include depressant drugs (narcotics, hypnotics, tranquillizers), hypothermia, reversible metabolic or endocrine disturbances and neuromuscular blockade. The other options are the brain-stem reflex findings that the tests themselves look for.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: In hospital, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) has failed and the patient has no circulation. For what minimum time must the doctor observe the patient to confirm absence of a central pulse and heart sounds?
options: 1 minute
2 minutes
5 minutes
15 minutes
mcq.explanation: Under the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges criteria, the person confirming death observes the individual for at least 5 minutes. During this time there must be no central pulse on palpation and no heart sounds on auscultation. The time of death is recorded once all criteria are met.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: A man remains in a vegetative state after a road-traffic head injury. After how long is the vegetative state judged 'permanent' under the Royal College of Physicians guidelines?
options: 12 months after the traumatic injury
3 months after the traumatic injury
6 months after the traumatic injury
24 months after the traumatic injury
mcq.explanation: The vegetative state is judged permanent if it persists for 12 months after traumatic brain injury. For non-traumatic causes the period is 6 months. Withdrawal of hydration and assisted nutrition can then be considered in the patient's best interests.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: A doctor stops all medical treatment of a terminally ill patient, so death occurs sooner. Which term describes this form of euthanasia?
options: Direct active euthanasia
Indirect active euthanasia
Dysthanasia
Passive euthanasia (orthothanasia)
mcq.explanation: Passive euthanasia, or orthothanasia, means restricting or stopping appropriate medical help for terminally ill patients, which hastens death. Active euthanasia involves an action that hastens death. Dysthanasia is the opposite, maximal prolongation of life.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

mcq.question: A body is found with a gunshot wound. The forensic expert establishes the category (violent) and type (mechanical injury) of death. Who determines the kind of death: homicide, suicide or accident?
options: The forensic expert, alone
Law-enforcement investigators or the court
The treating physician of the deceased
The hospital's head of department
mcq.explanation: Experts determine the category and type of death. The kind of death (homicide, suicide, accident) falls within the competence of law-enforcement officers or the court, because it depends on establishing intent.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

mcq.question: A death certificate reads: Ia Coma; Ib Subarachnoid haemorrhage; Ic Ruptured congenital aneurysm. Which entry is the most important for compiling mortality statistics?
options: Coma, listed on line Ia as the final state
Subarachnoid haemorrhage, listed on line Ib
Ruptured congenital aneurysm, listed on line Ic
Any condition that would be entered in Part II
mcq.explanation: In the WHO format the lowest disease in Part I is the primary pathological condition in the chain of events leading to death. It is the one used for national and international statistics. Coma is only a mode of death.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: A body found outside in freezing weather is stiff. After it is moved to the warm mortuary, the stiffness disappears, and true rigor appears several hours later. What explains the first stiffness?
options: Physical effect of cooling or freezing, not true rigor
True rigor that was broken during transport
Cadaveric rigidity caused by stress before death
Early autolysis of the muscle cells
mcq.explanation: When post-mortem cooling is extreme, stiffening may result from cooling or freezing rather than rigor. It disappears as the body warms. True rigor can then develop as the cellular chemical processes restart.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: A body is recovered from a river with weeds gripped tightly in the hand, although normal rigor would not yet be expected. Which term for this finding does Simpson's prefer?
options: Instantaneous rigor, because it appears at the moment of death
Cadaveric rigidity, because no satisfactory explanation exists
Primary flaccidity, because muscle tone is lost at death
Rigor mortis, because it is the same chemical process
mcq.explanation: Cadaveric rigidity has no scientifically satisfactory explanation and is clearly not the same chemical process as true rigor. The term 'instantaneous rigor' should no longer be used because it implies an equivalence with rigor.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: An examiner taps the biceps with a metal ruler. No raised ridge forms; a depression (dimple) appears at the site of the blow. Approximately how long after death was this reaction obtained?
options: About 1 hour after death
About 3 hours after death
About 6 hours after death
About 10–11 hours after death
mcq.explanation: The idiomuscular swelling gradually becomes lower and softer. About 10–11 hours after death a depression forms at the site of the blow instead of a ridge.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

mcq.question: On external examination a doctor finds a hard yellow-brown patch on the skin. A gauze pad soaked in warm saline is placed on it for 5–10 minutes. The patch softens and becomes paler. How should it be interpreted?
options: A vital abrasion that has begun to heal
A post-mortem parchment patch caused by drying
Hypostasis in the stage of imbibition
A bruise containing clotted extravasated blood
mcq.explanation: Parchment patches are post-mortem drying of damaged or thin-keratin skin. They soften and pale when moistened with warm saline or water, whereas vital abrasions do not change.

source.author: G‘iyosov Z.A.
source.title: Sud tibbiyoti (Tibbiyot oliy o‘quv yurtlari talabalari uchun darslik), Toshkent: Global Books nashriyoti

mcq.question: A body is found lying face down on a bed. It shows intense facial congestion, petechiae and pale areas around the nose and mouth. What is the most likely explanation for the pale areas?
options: Definite proof that the airways were smothered by hand
Pressure of the face against the bedding surface
Ante-mortem bruising caused by a blow to the face
Early putrefactive discoloration of the facial skin
mcq.explanation: Skin pressed against a firm surface cannot fill with settled blood, so it stays pale within the lividity. Pallor around the mouth and nose therefore does not necessarily indicate suffocation. The pathologist should still exclude pressure on the mouth, nose and neck by careful dissection.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: An unburied body lying in open air reaches a certain stage of decomposition after 1 week. All other factors being equal, how long would the same stage take if the body were buried in earth, according to Casper's ratio?
options: About 2 weeks
About 4 weeks
About 6 weeks
About 8 weeks
mcq.explanation: Casper's Law states that, other factors being equal, a body decomposes twice as fast in air as in water and eight times faster in air than in earth. One week in air therefore corresponds to about eight weeks in earth.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: A pathologist wants to estimate the post-mortem interval with Henssge's nomogram. Which three measurements does the method rely on?
options: Rectal temperature, ambient temperature and body weight
Rectal temperature, liver temperature and body height
Ambient temperature, degree of rigor and body weight
Skin temperature, stage of lividity and clothing type
mcq.explanation: Henssge's nomogram uses body (rectal) temperature, ambient temperature and body weight. Inaccuracy in any one of them degrades the result. Empirical corrective factors for clothing, air movement and water are then applied.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: A body recovered from wet ground after several months has a grey, firm, waxy shell that preserves the body shape. Which process underlies this change?
options: Desiccation of the tissues in dry, ventilated air
Spread of gut bacteria into the skin and blood vessels
Hydrolysis of body fat to a waxy, soap-like compound
Dehydration and tanning of tissues by humic acids
mcq.explanation: This is adipocere, a hydrolysis of body fat to a waxy soap-like compound. It is most common in wet conditions, such as submersion in water or burial in wet ground, and usually takes weeks to months.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

mcq.question: During an exhumation, poisoning is suspected. Which soil sampling approach is recommended for toxicological examination?
options: Samples only from the surface directly above the coffin
Samples around the coffin plus a control from a distant cemetery area
Samples only from beneath the coffin, without a control sample
A single sample from the cemetery entrance as the sole reference
mcq.explanation: Soil should be taken from above, below and to the sides of the coffin. A control sample from a distant part of the cemetery is also needed, together with samples of any fluid or solid material inside the coffin. These help answer later claims of contamination.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.

extras.text: Case analysis (Henssge nomogram): a 90 kg body is found with rectal temperature 26.4°C and ambient temperature 12°C. The book's worked example gives a time since death of 16 ± 1.8 hours, i.e. between about 13.2 and 18.8 hours before the measurement (95% confidence). Question: how would the range change if the ambient temperature had been wrongly recorded by 5°C? Answer: by at least 1 hour. The nomogram also assumes a naked body in still air, so corrective factors for clothing must be applied.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

extras.text: Memory aid (Casper's ratio): with free access of air, a body decomposes in about 1 unit of time, in water in 2 units and buried in earth in 8 units. Remember 'Air : Water : Earth = 1 : 2 : 8'. The slower decay in water and soil is explained by lower temperature and less oxygen. This applies only if all other factors are equal.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

extras.text: Interesting fact: a body dies cell by cell. Cortical neurons die after only 3-7 minutes without oxygen. White blood cells can still move up to 12 hours after cardiac arrest, and skin and bone cells can be cultured days later. For this reason, microscopic identification of a 'vital reaction' to injury is of doubtful reliability.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

extras.text: Case analysis (hypostasis or suffocation?): a body is found face down on a bed, with petechiae in the facial skin and conjunctivae and pale areas around the mouth and nose. Question: does this prove smothering? Answer: no. Hypostasis in the lax facial tissues can cause congestion and petechiae, and pallor appears where the face pressed on the bedding. The pathologist must exclude pressure on the mouth, nose and neck by dissection, looking for bruising and skeletal injury.

source.author: Payne-James J., Jones R., Karch S.B., Manlove J.
source.title: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, 13th ed.

extras.text: Memory aid (stages of livor mortis): Hypostasis = 'Highly mobile'. The stain blanches fully on pressure and moves if the body is turned. Stasis = 'Slowly shifting'. It only pales and partly moves. Imbibition = 'Immobile'. The colour does not change on pressure and the stain stays in place. Hypostasis is described as appearing at about 1.5-2 hours, with stasis from about 12 to 24 hours.
